subject: How to fit system of equations with Stan

messages.author: 6a121bb07651a8f3
messages.subject: How to fit system of equations with Stan
parts:
Hi, I've been questioning myself about the feasibility of fitting multiple equation systems with Stan. Let's say, for instance, the following:

y1 = b10 + b11*x_1
y2 = b20 + b21*y_1 + b_22*x_2

Is there any example available on how to code something like that?

Thanks for your time.

Tom

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to fit system of equations with Stan

> Hi, I've been questioning myself about the feasibility of fitting multiple equation systems with Stan. Let's say, for

>
> y1 = b10 + b11*x_1
> y2 = b20 + b21*y_1 + b_22*x_2
>
> Is there any example available on how to code something like that?

I'm not sure what you're asking for.

Stan doesn't yet have any implicit equation solvers, if
that's what you mean. So you can't write a system of equations
down as such and solve it. There are various linear algebra
solvers built in.

Is there a probabilistic model behind the y1 and
y[m] or the b[m,n]?

- Bob

Thanks for the quick answer, but I think I in fact did not make myself clear. Let me improve the question a bit: I was not thinking of solving algebraic equations. I was thinking of estimating recursive simultaneous equation models, i.e. when the dependent variable in equation one is independent variable in of equation two. So, yes, there is a probabilistic model behind the y and the coefficients.

Take for instance what would be the following coding for the model in Bugs:
y1[i] ~ N(mu1[i], tau1)
y2[i] ~ N(mu2[i], tau2)

mu1[i] ~ alpha[1] + g[1]*x1
mu2[i] ~ alpha[2] + b[1]*y1[i] + g[2]*x2

Is there a way to code a model like this in Stan?

Thank you for your time.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to fit system of equations with Stan
parts:
On Tuesday, August 6, 2013 1:27:51 PM UTC-4, Tomas Note wrote:
Take for instance what would be the following coding for the model in Bugs:
y1[i] ~ N(mu1[i], tau1)
y2[i] ~ N(mu2[i], tau2)

mu1[i] ~ alpha[1] + g[1]*x1
mu2[i] ~ alpha[2] + b[1]*y1[i] + g[2]*x2

Is there a way to code a model like this in Stan?

It would be pretty much the same way in Stan

parameters {
  vector[2] alpha;
  vector[2] g;
  real b;
  real<lower=0> sigma1;
  real<lower=0> sigma2;
}
model {
  vector[N] mu1;
  vector[N] mu2;
  mu1 <- alpha[1] + g[11 * x1;
  mu2 <- alpha[2] + b * y1 + g[2] * x2;
  y1 ~ normal(mu1, sigma1);
  y2 ~ normal(mu2, sigma2);
}

The main differences are that you can work with vectors in Stan and the normal density is parameterized with the standard deviation in Stan rather than the precision. The above assumes that y1 and y2 are conditionally independent, but if you want to relax that, then you can use a bivariate normal distribution, which can be parameterized with either a covariance matrix or a precision matrix.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to fit system of equations with Stan
parts:
On 8/6/13 3:05 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, August 6, 2013 1:27:51 PM UTC-4, Tomas Note wrote:
>
> Take for instance what would be the following coding for the model in Bugs:
> y1[i] ~ N(mu1[i], tau1)
> y2[i] ~ N(mu2[i], tau2)
>
> mu1[i] ~ alpha[1] + g[1]*x1
> mu2[i] ~ alpha[2] + b[1]*y1[i] + g[2]*x2
>
> Is there a way to code a model like this in Stan?

There's a section on regression modeling in the manual that
has examples of both doing this by hand and with matrices.

What Ben suggests below vectorizes a bit, which is more efficient.

>
> It would be pretty much the same way in Stan
>
> |
> parameters {
> vector[2] alpha;
> vector[2] g;
> real b;
> real<lower=0> sigma1;
> real<lower=0> sigma2;
> }
> model {
> vector[N] mu1;
> vector[N] mu2;
> mu1 <- alpha[1] + g[11 * x1;
> mu2 <- alpha[2] + b * y1 + g[2] * x2;
> y1 ~ normal(mu1, sigma1);
> y2 ~ normal(mu2, sigma2);
> }
> |

You might also want priors, though Stan can handle improper priors if
the posterior is proper.

Unlike in BUGS, but like in JAGS, you can use expressions directly
in the distributions, so your example model

> y1[i] ~ N(mu1[i], tau1)
> y2[i] ~ N(mu2[i], tau2)
>
> mu1[i] ~ alpha[1] + g[1]*x1
> mu2[i] ~ alpha[2] + b[1]*y1[i] + g[2]*x2

you can just write this:

y1 ~ normal(alpha[1] + g[1] * x1, sigma[1]);
y2 ~ normal(alpha[2] + b[1] * y1 + g[2] * x2, sigma[2]);

This'll work if x1 and x2 depend on i, too, as long as the x1
and y1 and x2 are declared as vector types.

- Bob

Nothing's mandatory in terms of form. As Daniel pointed out,
your issue was with the scope of the variable n. Stan scoping
in terms of loop variables works like in progamming languages
like Python and C++. (R's scoping is very odd, but your example
wouldn't have worked there, either.)

The SUR gives you covariance on the errors in a bunch of "seemingly
unrelated" regressions. I'm not sure how to set that up in your case where
there's an explicit dependence between y[n,1] and y[n,2]. For the normal,
I'm always surprised what you can do analytically...

Plain old SUR if you have predictors x[n] would be

y[n] ~ multi_normal(x[n] * beta, Sigma);

where

y[n] is a K-vector of outcomes

x[n] is a D-vector of predictors

beta is a D x K matrix of regression coefficients

Sigma is a K x K covariance matrix

We haven't vectorized multi_normal yet, but eventually this'll
just be y ~ multi_normal(x * beta, Sigma).

In hierarchical models, you can also put a covariance prior
on your regression coefficients.

I need to add sections on both of these to the manual. Soon,
we'll have all the regression models from Gelman and Hill's
regression book implemented (they do the hierarchical priors,
but I don't recall SUR).

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to fit system of equations with Stan
parts:
On Wednesday, August 7, 2013 1:51:55 AM UTC-4, Tomas Note wrote:
Finally, Ben mentioned that:

The above assumes that y1 and y2 are conditionally independent, but if you want to relax that, then you can use a bivariate normal distribution, which can be parameterized with either a covariance matrix or a precision matrix.

By relaxing such assumption you mean considering the possibility of correlation between disturbances in both equations (e.g. such as in a SUR model)? Is there any example on how to implement such a thing with the bivariate normal distribution parameterized with covariance matrix in Stan?

Although SUR allows non-zero correlations, this idea is not exclusive to SUR. In the 2x2 case, you can compose a covariance matrix from standard deviations and a correlation, like

parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma[2];
  real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho;
}
transformed parameters {
  cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
  Sigma[1,1] <- square(sigma[1]);
  Sigma[2,2] <- square(sigma[2]);
  Sigma[1,2] <- rho;
  Sigma[2,1] <- rho;
}

Then you just need priors on the two standard deviations and possible an informative prior on rho, along with the rest of your specification.

Ben
